doc.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995

title: What to call swing and classic jazz
summary: Rowe and Vaché discuss the lack of a good label for the music and how labels hinder more than help.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: A lot of the fellows we’ve been talking to who play swing or classic jazz or whatever we want to call it —
What do we want to call it? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

I was going to ask you. And we were talking earlier with Ralph Sutton and he refused to call it anything. And I don’t know what to call it because it’s — I mean swing is a big term, it could mean the big bands but it’s also a style of playing. Do you have any thoughts on the kind of music that you like to play?

I think it’s part of the problem we have in selling it is that we don’t have something we can call it. It’s not something that’s easily tagged. You draw from so many different inspirations and sources that it’s difficult to say I play one particular thing. That means it’s hard to sell, it’s hard for people who don’t know what it is to associate something. You say “swing” it means something different to you than it means to the guy that’s pumping your gasoline. We don’t have any specific term that really relates anything specific, because the music is this huge thing that encompasses almost all styles and influences.
Yeah, and it’s changed pretty quickly in the space of a hundred years, too, from —
New Orleans to what we have now. It’s interesting that you can still hear almost every phase of jazz being played live, somewhere.

Yeah, one of my favorite expression is “modern jazz is forty years old.” These labels don’t make much sense to me and I’m sure they don’t make sense to the guy on the street, who knows nothing about it. I don’t know whether they help or hinder. At this point I’m leaning more towards hindrance.
